items.stem: Match the property in List I with the distribution in List II.
items.explanation: A fixes the number of trials and counts successes, which is the binomial. B waits for the first success, which is the geometric. C waits for the rᵗʰ success and counts failures, which is the negative binomial. D is the n → ∞, p → 0 limit, which is the Poisson. This is June 2026 Q6; the marked option moved all four pairs.
pairs: A. Probability of the number of successes in a finite number of trials
B. Probability of the first success
C. Probability of the number of failures preceding the rᵗʰ success
D. Probability of success is infinitesimally small and the number of trials is very large

items.stem: The only discrete distribution possessing the memoryless property is:
items.explanation: P(X > m + n | X > m) = qⁿ = P(X > n) for the geometric, and the functional equation G(m+n) = G(m)G(n) forces G(n) = qⁿ, so no other discrete distribution can have the property. The exponential is its unique continuous counterpart.

items.stem: For a Poisson distribution, the mean and variance are:
items.explanation: Both equal λ. This equidispersion is the Poisson's signature and the reference point against which count data is called overdispersed or underdispersed.

items.stem: For a binomial distribution, the variance is:
items.explanation: The variance npq divided by the mean np is exactly q, which is strictly below 1 for any non-degenerate p. So a binomial is always underdispersed and can never be mistaken for a Poisson on this criterion.

items.stem: The negative binomial with r = 1 becomes:
items.explanation: Waiting for the first success is waiting for the rᵗʰ with r = 1. The moments agree: rq/p and rq/p² become q/p and q/p², the geometric's moments on the failures convention. Simulated at p = 0.3, both gave a mean of about 2.333.

items.stem: If X ~ B(n, p) with n → ∞, p → 0 and np = λ held fixed, the limiting distribution is:
items.explanation: This is the law of rare events, and it is statement D of June 2026 Q6. Numerically at λ = 2, the binomial P(X = 2) runs 0.2852, 0.2734 and 0.2709 for n = 20, 100 and 1000, against the Poisson(2) value 0.2707.

items.stem: The mean of a geometric distribution with parameter p, counting trials, is:
items.explanation: Counting trials gives support 1, 2, 3, … with mean 1/p and variance q/p². Counting FAILURES instead gives mean q/p, which is option C — so the convention must be read from the question. Option A is the variance.
items.check: With p = 0.3 the mean is 3.33 trials, which is the sensible reading of a roughly one-in-three chance.

items.stem: X₁ ~ Poisson(2) and X₂ ~ Poisson(3) are independent. Then X₁ + X₂ follows:
items.explanation: The rates add. The mgf makes it immediate: e^(2(eᵗ−1)) × e^(3(eᵗ−1)) = e^(5(eᵗ−1)). Option A multiplies the rates and option D averages them. Simulation gave mean 5.007 and variance 5.011.

items.stem: Sampling n items without replacement from a finite population and counting successes gives:
items.explanation: The binomial needs independent trials. Without replacement, drawing a success leaves proportionally fewer, so the draws are negatively dependent and the variance shrinks by the factor (N − n)/(N − 1). The MEANS of the two models agree, which is what lets the error survive casual checking.

items.stem: The mgf of a binomial B(n, p) is:
items.explanation: It is the binomial theorem with peᵗ in place of p. Check it at t = 0: (q + p)ⁿ = 1, as every mgf must give. Option B is the geometric's mgf and option A the Poisson's.

items.stem: For the negative binomial, the variance relative to the mean is:
items.explanation: The ratio is (rq/p²) ÷ (rq/p) = 1/p, which exceeds 1 for every p in (0,1) and does not involve r at all. The negative binomial is therefore always overdispersed, which is why it is the standard model for count data too variable for a Poisson.

items.stem: A count has mean 6 and variance 15. The family and its success probability are:
items.explanation: The ratio 15/6 = 2.5 exceeds 1, which rules out the binomial (ratio q < 1), the Poisson (exactly 1) and the hypergeometric (below q). Matching 1/p = 2.5 gives p = 0.4, and then mean rq/p = 1.5r = 6 forces r = 4. A negative binomial with r = 4, p = 0.4 has mean 6 and variance 15 exactly.
items.check: The ratio depends only on p, never on r — which is why it pins down the parameter even though the question withholds r.

items.stem: Consider the variance-to-mean ratio as a way of identifying a discrete family.
items.explanation: A is true: the ratio is q, strictly below 1. B is true: it is 1/p, above 1 for every p, and free of r. C is true and is the geometric's exception. D is false — the ratio also depends on nothing else, but a value of 1 does not prove the Poisson, since a geometric with p = 0.5 has mean 2 and variance 2.
statements: A binomial's variance-to-mean ratio is q, so it is always below 1.
A negative binomial's ratio is 1/p, so it is always above 1 whatever r is.
A geometric's ratio is q/p, which equals 1 exactly when p = 0.5.
A variance-to-mean ratio of exactly 1 proves the distribution is Poisson.

A.why: True. npq ÷ np = q, and q < 1 for any non-degenerate p, so a binomial can never be equidispersed.

B.why: True. (rq/p²) ÷ (rq/p) = 1/p, in which r cancels entirely, so r never affects whether a negative binomial is overdispersed.

C.why: True. q/p = 1 means q = p, so p = 0.5, where the mean and variance are both 2. Below 0.5 it is overdispersed and above 0.5 underdispersed.

D.why: False. It rules out the binomial and the negative binomial conclusively, but a geometric with p = 0.5 also has variance equal to its mean, so a ratio of 1 narrows the field rather than settling it.

items.stem: A lot of 50 contains 20 defectives and 10 items are drawn without replacement. The variance of the number of defectives found is:
items.explanation: The hypergeometric variance is npq(N−n)/(N−1) = 10 × 0.4 × 0.6 × 40/49 = 1.959. Option B is the binomial variance 2.40, which ignores the finite-population correction and overstates the spread by about 22%. Both models give the same mean of 4.
items.check: The correction factor 40/49 = 0.816 is well below 1, so the binomial is not a safe approximation here — the sample is 20% of the population, against a rule of thumb of 5%.

items.stem: A game succeeds with probability 0.1 per independent attempt. Given nine failures, the probability of success on the tenth attempt is:
items.explanation: The attempts are independent, so the tenth is unaffected by the first nine. Formally the geometric is memoryless: conditioning on past failures returns the original distribution. Option A is P(X > 10) = 0.9¹⁰ = 0.349 — more than a third are still waiting after ten attempts, which is why the mean of 1/p = 10 is not a deadline.
items.check: A conditional probability of success that exceeded the unconditional 0.1 would contradict independence, which was assumed in the question.

items.stem: The number of tails before the third head, in tosses of a fair coin, has mean and variance:
items.explanation: This is a negative binomial with r = 3 and p = 0.5, counting failures. Mean rq/p = 3 × 0.5/0.5 = 3 and variance rq/p² = 3 × 0.5/0.25 = 6. The ratio 6/3 = 2 = 1/p confirms it.
items.check: The ratio must be 1/p = 2 for a negative binomial with p = 0.5, which rules out option B at once.

items.stem: Consider the relationships between the discrete families.
items.explanation: A is true and is the r = 1 case. B is true and is the law of rare events. C is true: the correction (N−n)/(N−1) tends to 1. D is false — the binomial is closed under addition only when the success probability is the same, since (q₁+p₁eᵗ)ⁿ(q₂+p₂eᵗ)ⁿ is not of the form (q+peᵗ)^m unless p₁ = p₂.
statements: A negative binomial with r = 1 is a geometric.
A binomial with n → ∞, p → 0 and np = λ tends to a Poisson(λ).
A hypergeometric tends to a binomial as the population grows with K/N fixed.
The sum of two independent binomials with the same n is always binomial.

A.why: True. Waiting for the first success is waiting for the rᵗʰ with r = 1, and the moments rq/p and rq/p² reduce to the geometric's.

B.why: True. The mgf route is quickest: (1 + (λ/n)(eᵗ−1))ⁿ → e^(λ(eᵗ−1)). Numerically at λ = 2 the binomial P(X=2) approaches 0.2707 from 0.2852 at n = 20.

C.why: True. The finite-population correction (N−n)/(N−1) tends to 1, which is why the binomial approximation is safe when the sample is a small fraction of the population — under about 5% as a rule of thumb.

D.why: False unless the two success probabilities agree. Multiplying the mgfs gives (q₁+p₁eᵗ)ⁿ(q₂+p₂eᵗ)ⁿ, which is of binomial form only when p₁ = p₂, in which case the result is B(2n, p).

items.stem: For a geometric distribution counting trials, the variance exceeds the mean precisely when:
items.explanation: The ratio is (q/p²) ÷ (1/p) = q/p, and q/p > 1 means 1 − p > p, so p < 0.5. At p = 0.5 the mean and variance are both exactly 2, and at p = 0.7 the mean is 1.43 against a variance of 0.61. The claim in option C — that a geometric is always overdispersed — is the usual and incorrect summary.

items.stem: The functional equation G(m + n) = G(m)G(n) for G(n) = P(X > n) on the positive integers forces:
options: no restriction on the distribution of X
G(n) = 1/n, so X has no mean
G(n) = e^(−λn), so X is Poisson
G(n) = qⁿ, so X is geometric
items.explanation: Setting m = n = 1 gives G(2) = G(1)², and induction gives G(n) = G(1)ⁿ = qⁿ. Then P(X = n) = G(n−1) − G(n) = q^(n−1)(1 − q), the geometric with p = 1 − q. This is why the geometric is the UNIQUE memoryless discrete distribution, and the continuous analogue G(s+t) = G(s)G(t) forces the exponential.

items.stem: An inspector models counts from sampling without replacement as binomial and validates the model by checking average defective counts against the data. The validation passes. The best description is:
options: the error would have been caught by a larger sample
the binomial is correct, so there is no error
the means agree under both models, so the check cannot detect the error, which is in the variance
the hypergeometric and binomial differ only for small p
items.explanation: Each single draw is a success with probability K/N whether or not earlier draws are replaced, so the expected count is nK/N under both models. Replacement changes only the DEPENDENCE between draws, shrinking the variance by (N−n)/(N−1). A validation based on averages therefore confirms a model whose acceptance probabilities are wrong — and a larger sample makes the discrepancy worse, not better, since n/N grows.
